data.title: Japan Tobacco up 2% on Imperial Brands takeover talk
data.description: TOKYO, Nov 27 : Shares in Japan Tobacco climbed 2 per cent in early trading following a report it was considering partnering on a takeover of British cigarette maker Imperial Brands. US tobacco group Altria said on Thursday it was considering a possible all-cash bid for Imperial Brands and was discussing a deal involving acquiring part of the British company's business with another party. Tokyo-based JT is considering teaming up with a partner, Bloomberg News reported. JT declined to comment on the report. Japan's benchmark index was up 1 per cent in early trading. The moves could set the stage for one of the largest deals in tobacco industry history and reflect pressure on cigarette makers to find new growth avenues as smoking rates fall. Shares in Imperial, which said it had not received an approach but whose board would consider any proposal, jumped 13.8 per cent on Thursday, giving it a £25.90 billion ($33.93 billion) market valuation. Imperial would give a buyer a portfolio of established cigarette brands including Davidoff, Gauloises and Kool, which are sold in more than 100 markets. "This deal would make a lot of sense for both (Altria) and JT, in our view, while we believe the deal could be done without impacting the current credit ratings of either name," BTIG analyst Owen Bennett said in a note. JT, whose brands include Camel and Benson & Hedges, could take Imperial Brands assets in the US, Africa and the Middle East, Bennett said. JT, whose shareholders include the Japanese government, said last week it would record an $8.7 billion loss after losing control of its Russian subsidiaries.

data.title: US Marlboro maker Altria explores Imperial cash bid, possible carve-up
data.description: Nov 26 : US tobacco group Altria said on Thursday it was considering a possible all-cash bid for Imperial Brands and was discussing a deal involving part of the British tobacco group's business with another party, while Japan Tobacco was also reported to be weighing a bid. The moves potentially set the stage for one of the largest deals in tobacco industry history, combining three companies that together account for a significant share of the global cigarette market. Shares in London-listed Imperial jumped 13.8 per cent to 3,449 pence, giving it a market value of £25.90 billion ($33.93 billion). Depending on the structure of the deal, Altria could overtake British American Tobacco as the world's second-most valuable listed tobacco company, behind US Philip Morris International. Bloomberg News reported earlier on Thursday that Japan Tobacco was evaluating a potential acquisition of Imperial Brands, possibly with a partner, splitting up its assets around the world, citing people familiar with the matter. Analysts said a joint US-Japanese takeover could swerve antitrust objections and solve strategic challenges. The potential deal reflects mounting pressure on cigarette makers to find new growth avenues as smoking rates fall, and some struggle to compensate with newer nicotine products. Imperial said it had not had any discussions with, or received any approach from, Altria or a third party. "The Board is clear in its duty of aiming to maximise shareholder value and will consider any proposal, should one be made," it said in a statement. Japan Tobacco declined to comment on Bloomberg's report. IMPERIAL'S APPEAL TO BUYERS Imperial would give any buyer a portfolio of established cigarette brands spanning Europe and the United States, including Davidoff, Gauloises and Kool, sold in more than 100 markets. A deal could mark a return to international cigarette sales for Altria, two decades after it spun off its international division to focus on the United States. That move created Philip Morris International. Altria has not sold cigarettes or most other products outside the US since, leaving it more exposed than rivals to several key challenges in that market. Altria has a market value of $126.89 billion, while Japan Tobacco, which sells brands including Camel and Benson & Hedges in more than 130 markets, is valued at roughly $69.45 billion. A deal for Imperial Brands would rank among the largest recent acquisitions of a British company by an overseas buyer. London-listed firms have become attractive acquisition targets in recent years due to depressed valuations compared to their rivals listed on other European or US exchanges. Imperial Brands trades at just 8.3 times forward earnings compared with 12.6 times for Altria and 17.7 times for Japan Tobacco, LSEG data showed. The mega-deal would add to this year's global M&A haul, which has been expected by bankers to rival the record-breaking 2021 total even after a pullback in dealmaking in the wake of rising rates. SEARCHING FOR GROWTH Japan Tobacco, Altria and Imperial Brands have all lagged behind rivals such as PMI and British American Tobacco in expanding beyond traditional tobacco, with past efforts yielding mixed results. "Imperial and to a lesser extent (Japan Tobacco) and Altria are in a tough strategic spot, without the financial firepower to properly compete with (PMI and BAT) as the nicotine industry transitions from legacy cigarettes," Callum Elliott, analyst at Bernstein, said in a note. Last week, Imperial Brands, which makes Winston cigarettes, announced plans to cut up to 4,600 jobs, or nearly a fifth of its workforce. Altria and Japan Tobacco already have ties, having launched a joint venture in 2022 to grow newer product lines. Japan Tobacco has also been expanding its US tobacco business, particularly in cheaper labels that have been winning market share - a trend that has benefited Imperial's brands. Under UK takeover rules, Altria has until December 24 to make a firm offer or walk away. ($1 = 0.7634 pounds) ($1 = 159.1700 yen)

data.title: SAP considers at least 10,000 job cuts in AI restructuring, Bloomberg reports
data.description: Nov 26 : German software giant SAP is considering cutting at least 10,000 jobs in an AI-driven restructuring, Bloomberg News reported on Thursday, citing people familiar with the matter. Reuters could not independently verify the report. SAP, Europe's most valuable tech company, declined to commment. The restructuring would affect at least 9 per cent of SAP's global workforce, Bloomberg said, adding that the total number of job cuts could change after labour negotiations.

data.title: EU may vote on authorising Tesla assisted-driving system at Dec 15 meeting
data.description: STOCKHOLM, Nov 26 : A meeting of European Union countries on December 15 on whether to approve Tesla's assisted-driving system across the bloc may include a formal vote by member states on approval, according to a draft agenda published by the European Commission. Reuters reported on Wednesday that a meeting where the technology would be discussed had been postponed to December 15. On Thursday, in a draft agenda published for the meeting, the Commission explicitly raises the possibility of a vote for the first time, saying EU countries will further examine the Dutch request to grant type approval for the system "with possible vote".  The vote is a key step in Tesla's effort to roll out the technology across Europe, with nearly a dozen countries having followed the Dutch lead. But ​EU-wide approval requires ⁠backing from at least 15 of the bloc's 27 member states representing 65 per cent of its ​population.

data.title: Polish defence ministry to sign agreement with Palantir on Friday
data.description: WARSAW, Nov 26 : Poland's defence ministry will sign an agreement with Palantir Technologies Inc. on Friday to buy software that uses artificial intelligence to support decision-making processes, the ministry said on Thursday. • No other details of the agreement were provided in a statement • Poland started cooperation with Palantir in 2025, when it signed a memorandum of understanding covering artificial intelligence, information technology, and cybersecurity

data.title: Core inflation in Tokyo hits 16-month high, bolsters case for BOJ hike
data.description: TOKYO, Nov 27 : Annual core inflation in Japan's capital accelerated in November at the fastest pace in 16 months, highlighting mounting price pressure and bolstering the case for an interest rate hike as soon as next month. The data, widely regarded as a leading indicator of nationwide trends, will be among factors the Bank of Japan scrutinises in deciding whether to raise interest rates at its next two-day policy meeting ending on December 18. The core consumer price index, which includes prices of fuel but not fresh food, in Tokyo rose 2.9 per cent in November from a year earlier, data showed on Friday, compared with the median market forecast of 3.0 per cent. It followed a 2.6 per cent gain in October and marked the fastest year-on-year rise since July 2025. Core inflation thus stayed above the BOJ's 2 per cent target for three straight months, cementing the case for further hikes. While the increase was driven partly by an end to government utility subsidies, prices rose for a broad range of goods and services including food, daily necessities and hotel charges. "Core consumer inflation is expected to accelerate due to rising energy prices from the Middle East conflict and ensuing second-round effects," said Masato Koike, senior economist at Sompo Institute Plus. "If the current market instability stemming from concern over the AI and chip outlook persists, there's a chance the BOJ may forgo a rate hike in December. But our baseline projection is for the BOJ to proceed with one next month," he said. An index stripping away the effect of volatile fresh food and fuel prices, which is closely watched by the BOJ as a more accurate gauge of trend inflation, rose 2.5 per cent in November after a 2.6 per cent gain in October, the data showed. With stubbornly high energy costs and rising import costs from a weak yen adding to inflationary pressures, the BOJ raised its policy rate to 1.25 per cent in September after delivering a hike in June — a shorter interval than the roughly twice-a-year hikes seen in 2024 and 2025. The central bank kept rates steady in October, but said underlying inflation has roughly hit its 2 per cent target and signalled its readiness to continue hiking rates to prevent price growth from accelerating too much. A majority of analysts polled by Reuters expect the BOJ to raise rates in December and follow up with another hike by end-March. Many see the terminal rate at around 1.75 per cent or 2.0 per cent. Hawkish BOJ board member Naoki Tamura said on Thursday the central bank must respond swiftly to signs of an inflation overshoot, including by accelerating the pace of rate hikes.

data.title: New US tariffs: Limited near-term impact on Singapore, but analysts warn of lasting trade barriers
data.description: SINGAPORE: While the immediate hit from proposed United States tariffs may be limited, analysts warn that the move could signal a deeper shift toward higher trade barriers in the global economy, which could hurt small, open economies like Singapore over time. Their comments come after the Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR) on Wednesday (Nov 25) proposed a maximum potential tariff rate of 20 per cent, net of existing Section 301 tariffs, on Singapore's exports to the US – alongside similar actions targeting 13 other markets including China, Malaysia, Vietnam and Japan. But analysts stressed that the 20 per cent tariff on Singapore is a proposal that is still subject to public consultation. "This is still a proposed measure rather than a done deal," said Ms Selena Ling, chief economist at OCBC, who added that she would not overstate the macroeconomic impact for this reason. The bigger question is whether higher tariffs and trade barriers are becoming a more permanent feature of the global economy."More broadly, it is another reminder that even comprehensive trade agreements cannot entirely insulate countries from a more interventionist global trade environment," she said. As a major trade, logistics and financial hub, anything that slows regional trade and investment in the global environment will eventually “wash back” onto Singapore, said Ms Ling. Businesses would have to adjust to the new normal of prolonged policy uncertainty by reorganising supply chains around tariffs, national-security considerations and competing economic blocs, which reduces efficiency.  On Thursday, Singapore's Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry (METI) said it is disappointed with the proposed actions against Singapore. The USTR had released a report on investigations into the country's acts, policies and practices related to structural excess capacity and production in specific manufacturing sectors.  It added that the tariff rate could be adjusted to 10 per cent if Singapore reaches an agreement or addresses the concerns raised. METI said the findings did not take the structure of Singapore's economy into account. "Singapore's global trade surplus is a reflection of our outward- and market-oriented economy as well as our status as a trusted business and trading hub," it said in a statement. WHAT THE PROPOSED TARIFFS ACTUALLY AFFECT  Giving their early take on the USTR’s proposal, analysts told CNA that the tariffs could have a limited short-term impact on the Singapore economy, since the measures are still not set in stone. Ms Ling noted that the US has explicitly provided a pathway to a 10 per cent tariff if an agreement is reached, suggesting that there is "genuine room for negotiation". "I would therefore regard 20 per cent as an upper proposed rate rather than a foregone conclusion," said Ms Ling. Mr Chris Hampden, senior vice president at global procurement and supply chain consultancy Proxima, said Singapore's direct tariff exposure may be narrower than the headline suggests. He noted that semiconductors and pharmaceuticals were previously excluded from broad country tariffs. Certain electronics, aerospace products and energy products have also been excluded previously. Singapore's exports to the US that are affected by tariffs currently in place are worth about S$9.4 billion (US$7.3 billion), Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong told reporters on Thursday. With the latest proposed tariffs, the effective tariff rate on Singapore would be raised from 7.8 per cent to 10.3 per cent, he added.Apr 5, 2025: Trump’s Liberation Day tariffs take effect. Singapore goods are subjected to a 10 per cent baseline tax. Singapore's response: Set up a new task force to help businesses and workers and said it would not impose retaliatory tariffs on the US.  Aug 7, 2025: Revised US reciprocal tariffs take effect globally. Singapore’s 10 per cent levy rate remains unchanged. Feb 20, 2026: The Supreme Court of the United States strikes down Trump’s reciprocal tariffs. On the same day, the US president announces a 10 per cent tariff on all US imports for 150 days, starting from Feb 24. It expired on Jul 24, 2026. Jul 24, 2026: The US imposes a 12.5 per cent tariff on a range of Singapore’s exports following a US Section 301 investigation into 60 trading partners over their alleged failure to enforce bans on imports of goods produced with forced labour. Section 301 is designed to address unfair foreign practices affecting US commerce, and may be used to respond to “unjustifiable, unreasonable, or discriminatory foreign government practices that burden or restrict US commerce”, according to the US Trade Representative (USTR) website. About one-third of Singapore’s domestic exports to the US would be affected by the tariffs, according to the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry. Singapore's response: Maintained that it does not condone forced labour and has a comprehensive framework to tackle such practices domestically. It said it would continue to engage the USTR on the tariffs. Nov 25, 2026: The US proposes new tariffs on 14 major trading partners , including Singapore. The USTR proposed tariffs of up to 20 per cent on goods from Singapore, excluding certain products, taking into account existing Section 301 levies. The USTR added that it may adjust the tariff rate to 10 per cent if Singapore and Washington reach a reciprocal trade agreement or conclude other negotiations addressing the findings of the investigation. Singapore's response: METI said it would continue engaging the USTR and submit further comments during the upcoming public consultation period for the proposed tariffs. Mr Hampden said electronic components, specialty chemicals, healthcare products and some precision-engineered parts may potentially be exposed this time. "The final exposure will depend on the product annexes and precise US tariff classifications," he said. That view was echoed by Ms Lee Yen Nee, senior country risk analyst at BMI, which is owned by Fitch Solutions. She noted that the proposal contains a number of product exclusions. "That said, these will cushion the impact, not eliminate it. Singapore remains one of the more vulnerable economies in Asia to rising trade barriers given its heavy dependence on trade," she said. IS A 10% TARIFF POSSIBLE? It might be difficult for Singapore to negotiate the tariff rate down to 10 per cent, said Ms Lee of BMI. The US is concerned about policies that have helped Singapore to attract investment and build manufacturing industries despite having a very small domestic market, she said. Singapore would have to weigh the benefits of a lower US tariff with potentially weakening policies that have been central to its growth model, she added. "There is also a question of principle," Ms Lee said. "Making concessions under the threat of tariffs would sit uneasily with Singapore's long-standing support for a rules-based trading system." Ms Yue of Oxford Economics struck a more positive tone. She expects tariffs to come down eventually, though the timing and final rate remain uncertain. "The Trump administration has shown a willingness to use tariffs as negotiating leverage, so the outcome will depend on how far Singapore can address US concerns around manufacturing capacity, industrial policies and trade practices," she said.Mr Gan, who is also minister for energy, trade and industry (trade), said Singapore has always been very principled in its negotiations with trading partners like the US, while keeping Singapore's interests at the centre of discussions. The final figure may land somewhere between 10 per cent and 20 per cent, he added. "We also have to bear in mind that whatever agreement we arrive (at) or we achieve with the US, there will be give and take, there will be compromises, there will be trade-offs that we will need to be prepared to accept,” said Mr Gan. Speaking to journalists on Thursday, Mr Gan also defended Singapore's Central Provident Fund scheme, which the US claimed contributed to structural excess capacity because savings promotion depresses consumption and boosts the country's current account surplus. He said the CPF system is important, given Singapore's ageing society and lack of natural resources, and that the government encourages local consumption through other schemes such as Community Development Council vouchers.COMPARISONS WITH LIBERATION DAY TARIFFS Looking at the latest round of proposed levies alongside the Trump administration’s past tariffs, Ms Yue of Oxford Economics said the latest move signals a continuation of the US’ desire to use tariffs as a tool to pressure trading partners and address what it sees as unfair trade practices. But the tariffs differ in their legal basis and rationale, she said. Last April's tariffs, also known as the Liberation Day tariffs, were broad-based reciprocal measures, whereas the latest proposal follows an investigation into alleged excess manufacturing capacity and industrial policies. The US argues that Singapore's large manufacturing footprint and its role in global supply chains contribute to excess global manufacturing capacity, she said. "However, this is contested, particularly given Singapore's persistent bilateral trade deficit with the US," she added. For Singapore, another difference is that the proposed tariff rate this time is higher than its neighbours.  The maximum rate for Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand is 18 per cent, while Japan, South Korea and Taiwan are facing a tariff of up to 15 per cent. Last April, Singapore had a relative tariff advantage over regional competitors. When the tariff is finalised, it will raise the cost of Singapore exports into the US, and potentially squeeze exporters' margins, said OCBC's Ms Ling.  Manufacturing industries with significant US market exposure would be the most exposed, she added.Mr Hampden of Proxima noted that the 20 per cent figure is a proposed ceiling, not an additional 20 percentage points on top of Singapore's existing 12.5 per cent tariff. For goods already subject to the 12.5 per cent tariffs, there could be an additional 7.5 percentage points added, taking the combined rate to 20 per cent. Goods that are not subject to tariffs could face a larger increase, depending on the final product exemptions. Businesses should model the proposed rates as scenarios rather than assume that 20 per cent is the final outcome, he said. Singapore’s bigger challenge is to navigate the increasingly fragmented global trading environment, where protectionism and geopolitical tensions increasingly shape trade and investment decisions, said Ms Yue.  Singapore is exposed to this, as a highly trade-dependent economy, she noted.  But OCBC’s Ms Ling noted that there could be upsides. “Fragmentation can create opportunities for Singapore as a trusted, well-connected and politically stable business hub,” she said. “(That) arguably becomes more valuable when the external environment is less predictable.”

data.title: Japan's JERA enters talks with Anthropic, Meta to build data centres, Nikkei reports

data.title: Commentary: Black Friday is here, but what’s behind our need to chase bargains?
data.description: CARDIFF: Black Friday is a highly successful US export. The retail strategy designed to kickstart festive shopping has become a global phenomenon. But are the hype and the pressure (and the occasional fight over electrical hardware) worth it? After all, most products on offer during Black Friday are available at the same price (or even less) at other times of the year. So why do so many people still join in? Here are some of the marketing tricks and psychological drivers that help to explain the appeal of Black Friday.  MARKETING PUSH Offers that exist for a limited time period are among the oldest retail marketing tricks in the book. And there is plenty of research which shows that they reliably increase a shopper’s intention to buy. If we think a deal will disappear after Black Friday, the fear of missing out on a bargain can push us towards buying that air fryer or scented candle. Or we might buy it to avoid the potential feelings of regret that may come if we don’t. Price tags also have a big effect. Psychologists have shown that when making value judgments, the first number we see disproportionately shapes how we evaluate subsequent numbers. So when a price tag reads: “"Was £100 (US$131)! Now £60!”, the £100 figure is the one we latch on to. This makes £60 feel like a £40 saving rather than a £60 expense, even if the item was never really worth £100 in the first place. CONSUMER PULL While many people will be aware of these kinds of retail marketing tricks, they will still willingly participate in Black Friday. This may be partly due to its timing, but also to the psychological rewards that shopping could offer. In the northern hemisphere at least, Black Friday coincides with the “winter blues”, potentially offering a source of excitement as the days get colder and darker. We may also shop to improve our mood with a little “retail therapy”.One explanation for the effectiveness of retail therapy is that negative emotions often come from situations we cannot change. Making choices about what we want and then buying those things might help us to restore a feeling of personal control. Another reason is that buying generally might bring more positive than negative emotions. But studies have also shown that the temporary uplift from purchasing does not last as long as we often think it will. Landing a bargain can also make us feel good about ourselves. Being a “smart shopper” has been linked to a personal sense of achievement and pride when we secure a good deal. Buying things at a (genuine) discount can also demonstrate competence and good financial management to others. But that is not the only social appeal of Black Friday. Even the most independently minded consumer can be influenced by what other people do. And engaging in an activity at the same time as others, even among strangers, can temporarily enhance feelings of social connection.WHAT ARE WE REALLY BUYING? Despite the thrill of a bargain, or joining in with a commercial social event, what feels rewarding in the moment may not necessarily contribute to our longer-term wellbeing. Research in consumption has shown that spending money on things that fit our personality or that help us with personal goals might be a good idea. For example, an extrovert or someone looking to develop new connections will probably benefit more from spending money on social activities than buying a discounted item. But why we buy is as important as what we buy. In a recent study, my colleagues and I found that spending money in response to social pressure, to gain status or to seek others’ approval was linked to low wellbeing. So even experiences do not always bring more happiness. Our expectations can also mislead us. In another study I worked on, my colleagues and I found that people thought that buying new clothes would make them feel better about themselves than buying second-hand clothes. But it turned out that buying old and new clothes had pretty much the same effect. More broadly, research shows that focusing on economic gains and consumption brings a lower sense of wellbeing and is detrimental to our personal relationships. In contrast, choosing to live more simply or buying less is consistently linked with greater wellbeing. People who become less focused on material goals tend to become happier over time. So perhaps Black Friday should not simply be about how much money we are saving or how much temporary joy our purchases might bring us. Maybe it’s a time to reflect on what we gain from spending more money on more stuff, and whether there might be more sustainable and lasting alternatives. Olaya Moldes Andres is Senior Lecturer in Consumer Behaviour at Cardiff University. This commentary first appeared on The Conversation.

data.title: AI agents used in five cyber attacks in Switzerland, government says
data.description: ZURICH, Nov 26 : Five cyber attacks in the last few days in Switzerland used AI agents to target companies and operators of critical infrastructure, the Federal Office for Cybersecurity (BACS) said on Thursday. • In four of the five cases, the attacks were successful and systems were compromised, BACS said in a statement • Three operators of critical infrastructure were among those targeted, BACS said • These included providers of electricity, water, and telecommunications, Swiss public broadcaster SRF said • BACS did not give details of who could be behind the attacks • Companies are being advised to establish protection measures, including regular cyber tests, it said

data.title: Temu commits to changing some of its commercial practices in EU, Commission says
data.description: BRUSSELS, Nov 26 : Chinese e-commerce platform Temu has committed to bringing several of its commercial practices in line with EU consumer protection laws, the European Commission said on Thursday. "Temu's commitments concern a broad range of commercial practices that mislead consumers or unduly influence their purchasing decisions, including fake discounts, fake reviews, pressure selling, forced gamification, and missing and misleading information," the Commission said in a statement. Temu, which is owned by PDD Holdings, said it would provide clearer and more accessible information for customer support, prices, environmental claims and checkout, and would make refunds easier. Temu also committed to ending forced gamification features, like spinning the wheel to access the marketplace, and pressure-selling messages, the Commission said. A Temu spokesperson said the company was pleased to have reached a resolution. "We appreciate the constructive engagement throughout the process and will continue to strengthen transparency and improve the shopping experience for consumers across Europe." Countries will now monitor Temu's compliance with its commitments. Failing to comply could lead to fines of 4 per cent or more of Temu's annual turnover in the concerned member states.

data.title: Chubu Electric penalises 13 people over Hamaoka seismic data misconduct
data.description: TOKYO, Nov 26 : Chubu Electric Power said on Thursday it has penalised 13 people, including former Chairman Satoru Katsuno, over the falsification of seismic data at its Hamaoka nuclear power plant in Shizuoka prefecture in central Japan. • The company asked Katsuno to voluntarily return 50 per cent of his monthly remuneration for six months, while two employees were asked to resign, the company said in a statement • President Minoru Yasui said the company had taken strict disciplinary action based on the findings of an investigative committee and a comprehensive assessment of the individuals' responsibilities at the time • The utility also submitted a business improvement plan to the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry, including measures to reform its organizational culture and strengthen compliance and internal whistleblowing mechanisms • Chubu Electric received a business improvement order from the ministry on November 6 and was required to submit the plan • The company is seeking an external candidate for new chairman, to be appointed at its next shareholders' meeting, as well as a new head of its nuclear power division from either inside or outside the company. It aims to finalise the appointment of the new division head by year-end, Yasui said • The company also aims to formulate a new medium-term management plan by year-end, Yasui said

data.title: FIFA victim of cyber attack, files related to World Cup stake selloff unaffected
data.description: PARIS, Nov 26 : FIFA said on Thursday it had been the victim of a criminal cyberattack that gave unauthorised access to personal and business information. A person with direct knowledge of the matter told Reuters that no files from the abandoned FIFA Forward Enterprise project were accessed. "FIFA can confirm that it has been the victim of a criminal cyberattack resulting in unauthorised access to a limited set of personal and business information," a FIFA spokesperson told Reuters. FIFA strongly condemned the unlawful acquisition and publication of information, particularly personal data, adding that such actions were "a serious and unacceptable violation of privacy". FIFA did not say how many people or organisations were affected, when the attack took place or what the business information included. Its reference to publication did not say whether any data had appeared online, or where. The person with knowledge of the matter said less than 0.1 per cent of the total data held by world soccer's ruling body was affected. FIFA President Gianni Infantino said in July that his organisation had scrapped plans to sell a stake in the World Cup to private investors following a widespread backlash. The plan ‌had been to raise up to $4.2 billion by selling a 20 per cent stake in a new unit that would run FIFA events, including the World Cup.
